There were nine families of us hauling to that station and we were in and out of each other's kitchens the whole year round and I could name you every one of them, but you don't want names, you want the trouble, they always want the trouble.
6	
7	The station stood at the very top of the Hollow where the road bends and then goes to nothing but the ridge. It was a low building, whitewashed, cold as a spring house inside even in August, and it smelled of milk and steam and hot iron, and you could hear the engine going before you came round the last turn. Ansel Keddie ran it. He went up there in ninety-five, the year before they opened it, to get it ready, and he tested that first summer too, and he was still there when I was a girl big enough to ride on the wagon with my father, so you can count that up and see how long a man can stand in one room.

He wrote in it standing up at a slope desk by the window where the light came in. If a man came in and asked him what his milk had done, he did not have to hunt. He turned to the day and he read it off. He tested a thousand cans a week and never a blot in that book, and I heard my father say more than once that if the rest of the world kept its accounts the way Ansel Keddie kept his there would be no lawyers in Ashlin. 3	*Written out in numbered sections for the Association's own files, in the year after I laid down the minute book: from the minutes wherever the minutes will bear it, from my own recollection where they will not, and the two kept apart here as they ought to be kept.*
4	
5	**1. Of the organizing of the Association.** In 1889 the farmers of the Larrow Valley met at Larrow Green and organized themselves into the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association. Gideon Vose was elected the first president at that meeting and he held the office until 1911, which is twenty-two years, and no other man has held it so long. I did not see any of this. I was fourteen years old in 1889 and I came into the office as secretary in 1901, so for the first twelve years of the Association I am only a reader of its papers like anybody else, and a poorer reader than some, because the papers of exactly those years are the ones we have lost. The 1889–1892 minute book was lost when the office was moved in 1938. I say this here at the beginning because it governs everything I can and cannot write in the sections following.
6	
7	**2. Of the creamery at Larrow Green.** The main creamery was built at Larrow Green in 1891, on Larrow Creek, and it is the same building yet. Before it was built the members sold their milk where they could get a price for it and there was no common test and no common price, and every man's arithmetic was his own. The creamery ended that. Whatever is said of the Association afterward, it began as a plain remedy for a plain grievance, and I have never heard anybody in this valley say we should have been better without it.
8	
9	**3. Of the by-laws, and of Article VII.** Gideon Vose drafted the by-laws himself. He was not a lawyer and they read as a farmer wrote them, which is to their credit. The article that governs this history is the seventh, and because it is short and because it has been misquoted at me across this desk for forty years I set it down entire:
10	
11	> *Article VII. Every patron shall be paid for the milk he delivers according to the number of pounds of butter fat contained in it, ascertained by test, and not according to the weight of the milk; and the test of the station where he delivers shall govern.*
12	
13	Article VII was adopted at the annual meeting of 1892, the year after the creamery opened. What it did was this. Before it, a man was paid for what his cans weighed, and a hundred pounds of milk was a hundred pounds of milk whosever cow it came out of. After it, a man was paid for the fat that was found in his milk by a test made at the place where he delivered it, and the weight of his cans decided nothing by itself. The rule is a just rule and I have always said so: it pays a man for what he actually brings and not for the water that is naturally in it. But I would have the reader notice the last clause, which is the one nobody quotes. *The test of the station where he delivers shall govern.* Not the test of the creamery, not the average of the valley, not a test made over again anywhere else. The station's test, and no appeal from it. That clause is the hinge of the whole Ostrey Hollow business and it was written in 1892 by a man who died in 1917 and could not be asked about it afterward.
14	
15	**4. Of the officers in my time.** I was secretary from 1901 to 1940 and kept the minute book in my own hand throughout. Wilbur Teague came in as bookkeeper in 1905 and kept the ledgers. Hobart Sill was the buttermaker at Larrow Green and had the churn book and the cream receiving book. Selby Vose, son of the late president, was made manager in 1913 and served until 1938. I will say of the four of us that we were in that office together a very long time, that we were none of us idle, and that not one of us ever went up the valley and stood in the Ostrey Hollow station on a working morn]

638	*Two papers. The first is what he said, standing, before the board of arbitration at Ashlin on the seventeenth of March, 1925 — nine sentences and no more, taken down as he gave them. The second is a letter written at Ostrey Hollow later that spring; it was never sent, and was found among his papers.*
639	
640	**I. Statement to the board of arbitration, Ashlin, 17 March 1925.**
641	
642	> I have kept the test book of this station in my own hand since the station opened, and there is not a figure in it that I did not put there. I have set down the date, the patron, the pounds, the test and the fat, and where I have made an error I have drawn a line through it and put my letters against the line, and I have never written a figure over a figure. I have made the tests in the same order and at the same hour of every working day of every season. I have heard what the patrons say of me and I have heard what the officers say of me. Neither of them has come up that road on a working morning and stood at my elbow and watched the work done. I am asked to account for figures, and the figures are what I read and what I wrote and nothing besides. I am an old man and I have no other trade. I have tested as I was taught and as the state man saw me do it, thirty-one times a week for twenty-nine seasons, and I cannot tell you why the figures are what they are. I have never taken a pound of cream out of that station and there is not a man in this room who thinks I have when he is by himself.
643	
644	**II. Letter, written at Ostrey Hollow in the spring of 1925. Not sent.**
645	
646	I set this down because I could not say it in that room, where a man is allowed to answer and not allowed to explain, and because it seems to me that somebody ought to know how the work was done before everybody who did it is gone.
647	
648	The day began at half past five. The wagons came up the Hollow in the dark most of the year, and I had the intake room open and the lamps lit and the scale swinging free before the first of them was at the door. Every can went on the scale and the weight was called and written before the milk went anywhere else. That scale was tested by the state's man on his rounds and it was true, and I have never in twenty-nine seasons had a patron dispute a weight with me and be right.
649	
650	From each patron's milk I took a sample as it was weighed, and the samples went into his own jar, numbered to him and to nobody else, and the jar was made up over ten days before it was tested. On the testing morning the jar came out and was set in warm water until it was blood-warm right through, and then it was poured from vessel to vessel, and poured again, until the cream that had risen was carried down through the whole of it. A sample that is not warmed and mixed is worth nothing and a boy could tell you so.

3516	# Retelling 06 — Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector (retired), "Extracts from twenty-eight circuit books," with a covering note, 1936
3517	
3518	*Copied out this spring at the request of the state dairy office, from the pocket books I carried on the Ordell circuit. I have copied what is in them and put in nothing that is not.*
3519	
3520	**Covering note.** I took the Ordell circuit in nineteen hundred and seven and I have laid it down this year. It was fifty-odd plants in four counties — creameries, cheese factories, skimming stations, one or two little places that made butter three days a week and called themselves a creamery — and the state expected each of them seen at least once in the year and the doubtful ones oftener. I went by train where there was a train and by livery where there was not, and in the spring by neither, the roads up the side valleys being what they are in April. A man on this circuit learns the plants by their smells before he learns them by their names: the sour-sweet of a receiving platform in July, the lime and steam of a wash room, the flat cold nothing of a well-run cold room, which is the smell I liked best because it meant I would have no letter to write.

5	Members of the Association:
6	
7	It is thirteen years this spring, since 1913, that you have had the management of this Association in my hands, and I have stood up before you thirteen times to give an account of it. I mean to speak plainly about it, because plain speech is the only thing that has ever done this valley any good, and because a manager who talks around a difficulty leaves the difficulty exactly where he found it, with interest.
8	
9	Take the ordinary business first. The season opened wet and stayed wet into June, and the hauling was heavy on the horses and heavier on the men. The creamery at Larrow Green ran through the flush without a day lost, which is more than the creameries below us can say. Our butter has held its place with the trade that buys it, our churn room is clean, our ice went into the house early and lasted, and I have no complaint of any man on the payroll. The skimming station at Ostrey Hollow, seven miles up the valley, ran its season out and its cream came down to us daily and sweet. That is the whole of the ordinary business and I would to heaven it were the whole of the address.

12	
13	You know that in January of last year, 1925, the patrons of the Ostrey Hollow station laid a petition before this Association. You know its finding. The board found no cause established. It found no cause established against the station, against the office, or against any officer or servant of this Association, and I ask you to sit with that sentence a moment, because it is the only sentence in this business that was arrived at by men under oath with the books in front of them.

15	Having found no cause established, that board nevertheless awarded the Ostrey Hollow patrons thirty-eight hundred dollars, without admission, and charged it to the station account. This Association paid thirty-eight hundred dollars rather than let a body of its own members go on believing they had been used badly by their neighbors. There is not a business house in Ordell County that would have done it. We did it because we are not a business house; we are the farmers of this valley in company together, and a company that will not spend money to keep peace among its own members has not understood what it is for.

19	Water was going into cans at the head of that valley and it stopped when the Association began to look. The rise of 1924 is the measure of it. [tool_result: 1	# SKIFFLINE Municipal Ferry Scheduling Service, Interface Specification v2.4 — Kelmond Harbor Transit Authority, Engineering Standards Group (2023)
2	
3	## 1. Purpose
4	
5	SKIFFLINE is the authoritative scheduling and dispatch service for the Kelmond municipal ferry
6	network. It owns the published timetable, the live sailing board, the reservation ledger for
7	vehicle decks, and the tide-window constraints that govern the two shallow berths at Lowgate and
8	Ferrn Point. All consumer applications — the public web board, the terminal display units, the
9	deckhand handhelds, and the Authority's own operations console — read from SKIFFLINE and write
10	nothing except through the endpoints below.
11	
12	SKIFFLINE does **not** own vessel maintenance records, fare collection, or crew rostering. Those
13	live in MOORING (maintenance) and PAYWELL (fares) respectively and are joined by
14	`vessel_id` and `sailing_id`.
15	
16	Non-goals for v2.4: multi-operator federation, foot-passenger reservations, and any form of
17	dynamic pricing.
18	
19	## 2. Data model
20	
21	### 2.1 Route
22	
23	| field | type | notes |
24	|---|---|---|
25	| `route_id` | string, `RT-` + 3 digits | e.g. `RT-104` |
26	| `name` | string, ≤ 48 chars | e.g. "Lowgate – Ferrn Point" |
27	| `origin_berth` | berth_id | |
28	| `dest_berth` | berth_id | |
29	| `nominal_crossing_min` | integer, 4–180 | scheduled water time |
30	| `vehicle_capable` | boolean | false for the two passenger-only routes |
31	| `seasonal` | boolean | if true, `active_window` is required |
32	
33	The network currently defines nine routes, of which six are vehicle-capable.
34	
35	### 2.2 Berth
36	
37	| field | type | notes |
38	|---|---|---|
39	| `berth_id` | string, `BR-` + 2 digits | `BR-01` … `BR-14` |
40	| `name` | string | |
41	| `min_draft_m` | decimal(3,2) | 1.10 at Lowgate, 2.45 at Kelmond Main |
42	| `tide_gated` | boolean | true for `BR-03` and `BR-11` only |
43	| `ramp_class` | enum `A`\|`B`\|`C` | class C accepts no vehicle above 7.5 t |
44	
45	### 2.3 Sailing
46	
47	A **sailing** is one scheduled departure of one vessel on one route.
48	
49	| field | type | notes |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| `sailing_id` | string, `SL-` + 8 digits | monotonic, not sequential |
52	| `route_id` | route_id | |
53	| `vessel_id` | string, `VS-` + 3 digits | |
54	| `scheduled_depart` | RFC 3339, always with offset | |
55	| `state` | enum | see 2.4 |
56	| `deck_slots_total` | integer, 0–86 | |
57	| `deck_slots_held` | integer | ≤ `deck_slots_total` |
58	| `tide_window` | object or null | `{opens, closes}`, null if berths not gated |
59	| `etag` | opaque string | required for all mutations |
60	
61	### 2.4 Sailing state machine
62	
63	```
64	PLANNED ──publish──> PUBLISHED ──board──> BOARDING ──depart──> UNDERWAY ──arrive──> ARRIVED
65	   │                     │                    │
66	   └──cancel──> CANCELLED┴────cancel──────────┘
67	```
68	
69	`UNDERWAY` may not transition to `CANCELLED`. A sailing in `ARRIVED` is immutable except for the
70	`actual_arrive` field, which may be corrected once within 90 minutes by an operator holding the
71	`sched.correct` scope.
72	
73	### 2.5 Deck reservation
74	
75	| field | type | notes |
76	|---|---|---|
77	| `res_id` | string, `RS-` + 10 chars, base32 | |
78	| `sailing_id` | sailing_id | |
79	| `plate` | string, ≤ 10 chars, upper | normalized: strip spaces and hyphens |
80	| `length_class` | enum `S`\|`M`\|`L`\|`XL` | consumes 1, 1, 2, 3 deck slots |
81	| `hold_expires` | RFC 3339 | default now + 20 min |
82	| `confirmed` | boolean | |
83	
84	## 3. Endpoints
85	
86	Base path `/v2`. All requests carry `X-Skiffline-Key`. All responses are `application/json`
87	with `Content-Language: en`.
88	
89	### 3.1 `GET /v2/routes`
90	
91	Returns all routes. Query params: `vehicle_capable` (bool), `active_on` (date).
92	Cacheable for 3600 s.
93	
94	### 3.2 `GET /v2/sailings`
95	
96	Required: `route_id`, `from` (RFC 3339), `to` (RFC 3339). The span `to − from` may not exceed
97	14 days; a]

Error code for a sailings-query span exceeding 14 days is SKF-2201.

Sent to Corliss City by the afternoon train for antitoxin, which did not arrive until the 24th on account of the agent's error in the telegram. Child improved from the 25th. 2	
3	## 1. Purpose
4	
5	Purlwright is a desktop editor for knitting and crochet charts. The plugin API exists so that
6	third parties can add stitch dictionaries, chart transformations, gauge calculators, exporters,
7	and live validators without forking the editor.
8	
9	A plugin is a directory containing a `plugin.toml` manifest and one or more JavaScript modules.
10	Plugins run in a worker isolate with no filesystem or network access; all effects are requested
11	through the host bridge described in §5.
12	
13	This document covers API level **31**. Level 31 is source-compatible with level 29 and drops the
14	level-27 `chart.rawCells()` accessor.
15	
16	## 2. Manifest
17	
18	```toml
19	[plugin]
20	id            = "org.tinsel.cablewright"
21	name          = "Cablewright"
22	version       = "1.4.2"
23	api_level     = 31
24	entry         = "main.js"
25	
26	[capabilities]
27	stitch_dictionary = true
28	transforms        = ["mirror", "reflow"]
29	exporters         = ["pdf", "svg"]
30	validators        = ["gauge", "cable_span"]
31	
32	[limits]
33	max_cells_per_pass = 250000
34	max_wall_ms        = 4000
35	```
36	
37	`id` must be a reverse-DNS string of 6 to 96 characters. Duplicate `id` values cause the later
38	plugin to be skipped with diagnostic `PW-0102`.
39	
40	If `api_level` is below 29 the plugin is refused outright (`PW-0104`). If it is above the host's
41	level the plugin loads in **degraded mode**: only `stitch_dictionary` capabilities are honored.
42	
43	## 3. Data model
44	
45	### 3.1 Chart
46	
47	A chart is a rectangular grid of cells addressed `(row, col)` with row 1 at the **bottom** and
48	column 1 at the **right**, matching the direction of work. Charts carry:
49	
50	| field | type | notes |
51	|---|---|---|
52	| `id` | uuid v4 | |
53	| `rows` | int, 1–4096 | |
54	| `cols` | int, 1–1024 | |
55	| `gauge` | `{stitches_per_10cm, rows_per_10cm}` | decimals, 2 dp |
56	| `flat` | bool | false means worked in the round |
57	| `repeat` | `{row_from, row_to, col_from, col_to}` or null | |
58	| `revision` | int | increments on every committed mutation |
59	
60	### 3.2 Cell
61	
62	```ts
63	interface Cell {
64	  readonly row: number;
65	  readonly col: number;
66	  symbol: SymbolRef;      // e.g. "k", "p", "c4f", "yo", "ssk"
67	  colorIndex: number;     // 0-based into chart palette, max 24 entries
68	  noSpan?: boolean;       // set on the trailing cells of a multi-cell symbol
69	}
70	```
71	
72	A symbol whose `width` exceeds 1 occupies its anchor cell plus `width − 1` trailing cells with
73	`noSpan: true`. Writing a symbol over a trailing cell without first clearing its anchor raises
74	`PW-2210`.
75	
76	### 3.3 SymbolRef and dictionaries
77	
78	```ts
79	interface StitchSymbol {
80	  ref: string;            // 1–12 chars, [a-z0-9_]
81	  label: string;          // shown in the legend
82	  width: number;          // 1–8
83	  consumes: number;       // stitches consumed from the row below
84	  produces: number;       // stitches produced
85	  glyph: string;          // inline SVG path data, ≤ 2048 chars
86	}
87	```
88	
89	The editor enforces the row-balance rule: for every row *r*, the sum of `consumes` over row *r*
90	must equal the sum of `produces` over row *r − 1*, with row 0 taken as the cast-on count. A
91	violation is a **soft** error and is surfaced as `PW-3302` on the affected row rather than
92	blocking the edit.

[tool_result: 1	# Retelling 16 — Dr. Roland Kepp, "The bog meadows and the milk," a paper read before the Ordell County Farm Club, 1926
2	
3	*A veterinary surgeon of thirty years' practice brings the agricultural literature to bear on an old local grievance, and the discussion from the floor is appended as taken down by the club's secretary.*
4	
5	**THE BOG MEADOWS AND THE MILK**
6	
7	*By Roland Kepp, V.S., of Ashlin*
8	
9	Mr. Chairman and gentlemen: it is my habit, when I am called to a herd that is doing badly, to ask first what the cattle are standing on. I have found in thirty years that the answer to nine cases in ten is under the animal's feet, and that the tenth is in the water she drinks. I want to put before you this evening a question that has been in this county longer than I have practiced in it, and that has been dealt with hitherto by opinion, by grumbling, and by the naming of names. It deserves better. It is a question of soil, of herbage, and of the mineral economy of the cow, and I mean to treat it as such.
10	
11	**The land.** A wet bottom is not a rich meadow with too much water in it. It is a distinct kind of ground with a distinct kind of chemistry, and the water is the least part of it. Where drainage is wanting, the year's growth does not rot down as it does on a hill field; it lies sour, and the soil that results is an acid soil, poor in lime, and poor in the phosphates. On such ground the sweet grasses will not hold. They are crowded out within a few seasons by sedge and rush and the coarse tussock grasses, which want nothing better than sour wet land and will take it over completely if you let them. That herbage carries bulk and it carries water. What it does not carry, in any quantity worth the name, is lime or phosphorus, and it is cut late because such ground cannot be got onto early, and late cutting takes out what little was in it.
12	
13	**What the cow does with such keep.** Now consider the animal. A cow in milk is a manufactory working on a narrow margin, and she is obliged to find the material of her milk somewhere. If her ration is short of the minerals, she does not simply give less; she robs her own frame to make good, and she goes on robbing it until she cannot. You will see the consequences in any wet-meadow herd in this county and I have seen them in all of them. The stock come out of the winter feeding thin over the loin and rough in the coat. They are slow to come to condition in the spring. They are ready subjects for every disorder of the digestion in the fall of the year, and I am oftener called to that class of trouble on wet land than on any other. They breed later. Their feet are worse.
14	
15	They will milk, gentlemen. Wet land is generous of flow and no man on a bog meadow ever complained that his pail was light. But what is in the pail is another matter, and the fat is the first thing to suffer, because the fat is the dearest thing the cow makes and it is the first economy she practices when she is pressed.
16	
17	**The measure of it.** I have gone about this county for thirty years and I have kept my eyes open. The wet bottoms of this county yield a milk poorer in fat by a fifth of a point and every practical man knows it. Set the hill herds of this county against the bottom herds and you will find that difference, farm for farm, wherever you look for it, and the difference does not depend on the breed, on the man, or on the barn. It depends on the ground.
18	
19	**Hessel Bottom.** I come to the case which is in everybody's mind. Hessel Bottom, under Ostrey Hollow, is the completest example of wet meadow in this county. Six farms cut hay and pasture stock upon it. It lies along the creek; the springs come out at the foot of the slope and run in it the year round; a part of it is under water every spring and is not fit to be walked on until well into May. Its hay is sedge hay, and on those farms it is the winter dependence and very nearly the whole of it.

2	
3	## 1. Purpose and scope
4	
5	BSWP is a compact, half-duplex message protocol for battery-powered environmental sensors
6	deployed inside commercial glasshouses. It targets nodes with 32 KB of flash and no real-time
7	clock, connected over a shared two-wire bus of up to 400 m with as many as 96 nodes per segment.
8	
9	BSWP/2.0 supersedes 1.3. The framing is deliberately unchanged so that a 1.3 gateway can pass
10	2.0 traffic through without understanding it; the payload registers are renumbered and are not
11	compatible.
12	
13	Out of scope: over-the-air firmware delivery (see TN-0051), irrigation valve actuation, and any
14	form of encryption. BSWP assumes a physically trusted bus.
15	
16	## 2. Framing
17	
18	Every frame is a byte sequence:
19	
20	```
21	+------+------+------+--------+-----------+--------+------+
22	| 0xB5 | LEN  | ADDR | OPCODE | PAYLOAD   | CRC16  | 0x5B |
23	+------+------+------+--------+-----------+--------+------+
24	   1      1      1       1       0..247       2       1
25	```
26	
27	- `0xB5` start delimiter, `0x5B` end delimiter.
28	- `LEN` counts `ADDR` through `PAYLOAD` inclusive, so `LEN` ranges 3..250.
29	- `ADDR` is the node address, 0x01–0x60. `0x00` is the gateway. `0xFF` is broadcast.
30	- `CRC16` is CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE over `LEN` through `PAYLOAD`, transmitted big-endian.
31	- Byte stuffing: any `0xB5` or `0x5B` appearing inside `LEN..CRC16` is escaped as `0x7D` followed
32	  by the byte XOR `0x20`. `0x7D` itself is escaped the same way.
33	
34	Maximum on-wire frame length after stuffing is 508 bytes. A receiver that has consumed 508 bytes
35	without seeing `0x5B` discards and resynchronizes on the next `0xB5`.
36	
37	Bus rate is 19200 baud, 8N1. Inter-frame gap is a minimum of 3 character times (1.56 ms).
38	
39	## 3. Addressing and discovery
40	
41	Nodes ship with `ADDR = 0x00` (unconfigured) and a 6-byte factory serial. On power-up an
42	unconfigured node listens only; it never transmits unbidden.
43	
44	The gateway discovers nodes with a binary-search sweep over the serial space:
45	
46	1. Gateway broadcasts `OP_PROBE` (0x11) with a 6-byte prefix and a prefix length in bits.
47	2. Every unconfigured node whose serial matches the prefix replies after a jitter of
48	   `serial[5] mod 24` milliseconds with `OP_HERE` (0x12) carrying its full serial.
49	3. Collisions are detected by CRC failure; the gateway lengthens the prefix by one bit and
50	   repeats. Worst case is 48 rounds.
51	4. Gateway assigns an address with `OP_ADOPT` (0x13), payload = serial (6 bytes) + new `ADDR`
52	   (1 byte). The node writes it to flash and replies `OP_ACK`.
53	
54	A node that receives `OP_ADOPT` while already addressed replies `ERR_ADOPTED` (see §6).
55	
56	## 4. Register model
57	
58	Each node exposes a flat register file. Registers are 16-bit addressed, 1–8 bytes wide, and
59	carry a type tag in their descriptor.
60	
61	| reg | name | width | type | units | notes |
62	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
63	| `0x0100` | `AIR_TEMP` | 2 | int16 | 0.01 °C | −4000..8500 |
64	| `0x0102` | `AIR_RH` | 2 | uint16 | 0.01 % | 0..10000 |
65	| `0x0104` | `CO2_PPM` | 2 | uint16 | ppm | 0..40000, 0xFFFF = over-range |
66	| `0x0106` | `PAR` | 4 | uint32 | µmol·m⁻²·s⁻¹ ×1000 | |
67	| `0x0108` | `LEAF_WET` | 1 | uint8 | 0..100 | derived, not measured |
68	| `0x0110` | `SOIL_VWC_A` | 2 | uint16 | 0.01 % | probe A |
69	| `0x0112` | `SOIL_VWC_B` | 2 | uint16 | 0.01 % | probe B, 0xFFFE = absent |
70	| `0x0114` | `SOIL_EC` | 2 | uint16 | µS/cm | |
71	| `0x0200` | `BATT_MV` | 2 | uint16 | mV | |
72	| `0x0202` | `UPTIME_S` | 4 | uint32 | s | wraps at 2^32 |

### 1. The Station at Ostrey Hollow

In 1889 farmers of the Larrow Valley met at Larrow Green and organized the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association, building its main creamery there in 1891. Article 7 of its by-laws fixed the principle that mattered most later: patrons were paid by the butterfat their milk tested at, not by its weight, and the test made at the delivery station governed pay. In the winter of 1895–96 the Association built a skimming station seven miles up-valley at Ostrey Hollow to serve the farms of Hessel Bottom. It opened 4 May 1896, at first borrowing its testing glass from Larrow Green. Ansel Keddie was tester and separator man from the day it opened, a post he held for twenty-nine seasons.

The station's own glassware — six dozen milk-test pipettes graduated at 17.6 cc, twelve dozen test bottles, an acid measure, and a four-bottle hand tester — was ordered from Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoiced 14 April 1897 at a total of $77.93, and put into use 1 May 1897. Two later retrospective accounts (a clerk's 1953 memoir and a state college bulletin) instead place this installation in 1898. I resolve this for 1897: the Ammon & Sons invoice is a contemporaneous business record, and Orra Keddie, the tester's wife, wrote in her diary that same day, "A. says the station's own glass came up and they are done borrowing of Larrow Green" — a same-day entry outranks two decades-later memories.

This is the origin point of everything that follows: a station built to serve a handful of wet-ground farms, run for a generation by one man, on glassware bought once in 1897 and not replaced until it was condemned twenty-six years later.
